I farm in Quzhou County, Hebei, on the North China Plain, so I will keep to the pattern I trust most: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. At my age and with the way I work, I do not want a complicated mix of crops that needs too much sorting, marketing, or special management. Wheat and maize fit my machinery, my labor, my experience, and the local water and weather pattern. They also spread the work across the year in a way I can handle.

I will put essentially all my main field area into this wheat-maize rotation. For winter wheat, I will use improved seed because I want stable emergence, lodging resistance, and dependable yield, but I do not need expensive specialty seed. I will prepare the land with rotary tillage after the previous crop residues are handled, sow on time in autumn, apply most phosphorus and part of nitrogen as base fertilizer, then topdress nitrogen in spring. I will irrigate at the stages that matter most for me, especially overwintering recovery and grain filling if moisture is short. I will spray only as needed for aphids, rust, or other common disease and insect pressure, but I will still plan for a couple of applications because I know the crop usually needs protection.

After wheat harvest, I will quickly turn to summer maize on the same area so I do not lose soil moisture or planting time. For maize, I will use hybrid seed because that is the crop where hybrid vigor pays off clearly in my conditions. I will keep fertilization moderate but solid, with nitrogen carrying the biggest share, and I will manage the field with rotary tillage or very shallow seedbed preparation so I can plant fast after wheat. Irrigation for maize will be limited to the key periods if rainfall is not enough, because water is always something I watch carefully. I will keep pesticide use controlled, mainly for borers, armyworms, or leaf disease when pressure appears. My goal is not maximum possible yield at any cost; it is a steady, manageable, profitable year using the rotation I know best.
